This paper delves into the fundamental tradeoff between generalization and identification in intelligent systems, arguing that this tension arises from the inherent limitations of finite semantic resolution. The authors propose that any model with a finite capacity to represent semantic similarity will inevitably face a tradeoff between its ability to generalize to novel situations and its ability to precisely identify specific instances. The core of their argument rests on the idea that a model's representational space has a limited resolution, meaning that distinctions between concepts can only be made up to a certain level of granularity. This limitation, they contend, creates a Pareto front linking a model's probability of correct generalization ($p_S$) and identification ($p_I$). The authors develop a theoretical framework to quantify this tradeoff, deriving closed-form expressions that describe the relationship between $p_S$ and $p_I$ under various conditions, including different input spaces and parallel processing scenarios. A key prediction of their theory is a sharp $1/n$ collapse in the capacity to process multiple inputs simultaneously, where $n$ is the number of inputs. This prediction stems from the idea that as the number of items increases, the probability of all items falling within the resolution limit of the model decreases rapidly. These experiments demonstrate that the observed tradeoff is not merely a theoretical construct but a fundamental constraint on representational systems. The authors show that the empirical trajectories of these models closely match the theoretical predictions, providing strong support for their framework. The paper's central contribution lies in its rigorous mathematical formulation of the generalization-identification tradeoff, its clear articulation of the role of finite semantic resolution, and its empirical validation across diverse model architectures. By linking the tradeoff to the concept of finite semantic resolution, the authors offer a novel perspective on the limitations of representational systems, suggesting that the tradeoff is not simply a matter of model capacity but a fundamental property of any system that represents meaning. The paper's findings have significant implications for our understanding of the limitations of intelligent systems and for the design of more efficient and robust models.
